analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license and dealer-recorded sale to buy or own a handgun or certain semiautomatic rifles.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2026 with two sponsors and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, the bill has received no hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to own a handgun or a detachable-magazine semiautomatic rifle without a firearm owner license issued after a background check, fingerprints, and a photo application. Every sale or transfer of those guns would have to go through a licensed dealer and be reported into a new federal record-of-sale system, and owners would face new duties to report lost or stolen guns, secure guns from children, and update their addresses. Penalties for unlicensed possession run up to 10 years in prison.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities with high gun violence: the bill's findings cite 44,000 U.S. gun deaths in 2024, with Black and Latino children dying at far higher rates than white children, and aim to keep guns from prohibited buyers and make crime guns traceable. Police would gain a federal record of every covered gun sale to trace guns used in crime, and the Attorney General would build a firearm-injury research clearinghouse.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities hit hardest by gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Would require anyone owning a handgun or detachable-magazine semiautomatic rifle to hold a federal license issued after a fingerprint-based background check, generally barring people under 21 (except with parental consent), people recently committed to mental health facilities, and people with recent violent misdemeanors or protection orders against them.

Would require every sale or transfer of a covered gun to run through a licensed dealer who verifies the buyer's license and reports the transaction to the Attorney General within 14 days, creating a federal record-of-sale system for tracing crime guns.

Would criminalize failing to report a lost or stolen gun within 72 hours, failing to update an address within 60 days, and keeping a loaded gun accessible to a child who then causes death or serious injury, with exceptions for secured storage and lawful self-defense.
Would cap the federal license fee at $10 and let states run their own Attorney General-certified licensing and record systems instead of the federal one.

analysis.who_pays: Tens of millions of current gun owners would need a federal license — photo, rolled fingerprints, and mental-health record releases — to keep guns they already own, with a two-year window before the requirement bites, and would face up to 10 years in prison for unlicensed possession. The firearms industry would bear new reporting, inspection, and transfer-intermediary duties, and taxpayers would fund the Attorney General's licensing and record systems.

drawbacks.text: Unlicensed possession of a covered gun would carry up to 10 years in prison, and even failing to report a change of address within 60 days would be a crime — meaning millions of otherwise law-abiding owners could face felony-level exposure over paperwork.

The bill repeals the existing federal prohibition on establishing a firearms registration system and builds a national record-of-sale database, and a person whose license is denied or revoked must transfer away any covered gun within 48 hours — provisions gun-rights supporters regard as a backdoor national registry enabling future confiscation.

The $10 fee cap does not cover the real costs of applying, which fall on the applicant: passport photos, rolled fingerprints, and — for anyone who was ever a mental-health patient — a paid evaluation by a physician or clinical psychologist; broad disqualifiers like any non-traffic misdemeanor conviction could deny many applicants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill takes on a documented problem — its own findings cite 44,000 U.S. gun deaths in 2024 — and licensing-plus-records is among the policies researchers associate with fewer gun deaths. But as written it is blunt: it converts possession of the most common kinds of guns into a licensing offense punishable by up to 10 years, concentrates sweeping denial-and-revocation power in the Attorney General, and creates a de facto national registry, which is why it has attracted only two sponsors in a Republican-run House. A narrower bill covering the same safety goals with lighter penalties would likely fare better on both policy and politics.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 2026 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which has not acted on it since.

narrative.text: Representative Jonathan Jackson of Illinois introduced the bill on June 30, 2026, with Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton as the only cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day it was introduced.
Since the referral, the committee has taken no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill has sat without movement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nobody has had to fight this bill: firearms makers and dealers, and gun owners opposed to licensing and registration, are better off because the bill has not moved, while communities the bill aimed to protect have gained nothing yet either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of gun licensing, for now

for.name: Rep. Jonathan Jackson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 30, 2026, naming it for Blair Holt, a Chicago student killed on a bus in 2007.

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral on June 30, 2026 and has never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Both of the bill's backers are Democrats, and none of the 223 House Republicans has signed on; no vote has occurred.

industries.note: Every sale or private transfer of a covered gun would have to run through a licensed dealer, who verifies the buyer's license, records a tracking number, and files a report — making dealers the mandatory paid intermediaries for all such transfers even as they take on new record-keeping and inspection duties.

Manufacturers would face reporting of production and sales figures, business-hours inspections, and the Attorney General's power to order a halt to sales of guns transferred in violation of the law, and licensing could shrink the market for handguns and detachable-magazine rifles. The industry's interest in unrestricted sales runs against the bill's public-safety aim, though dealer-intermediary rules also channel business through licensed channels.

The bill carves out exemptions for supervised range use, hunting, safety courses, and ceremonies, but ordinary members would still need federal licenses to keep handguns at home, and training organizations are folded into the bill's recognized-course framework.

analysis.trajectory: With two sponsors, zero Republican support, and no committee action more than two months after referral in a session that ends January 3, 2027, the bill is all but certain to die quietly in the Judiciary Committee without a vote, as federal gun-licensing bills have in past Congresses.
